title: Early Greek Mathematics and Astronomy
orientation: This chapter surveys Greek mathematics and astronomy from Thales through the end of the Hellenistic period, treated not for their own sake but for their close relationship to Greek philosophy, above all Plato's. Russell argues that Greek preeminence 'appears more clearly in mathematics and astronomy than in anything else,' tracing the invention of rigorous mathematical demonstration, the near-discovery of the calculus (the method of exhaustion), Euclid's axiomatic system, and a sequence of increasingly accurate astronomical hypotheses that culminate, remarkably early, in Aristarchus's full heliocentric theory -- a theory ancient astronomy then rejected for nearly two thousand years.
historical_background: Russell notes the Greeks derived practical 'rules of thumb' in mathematics from Egypt and long-accumulated observational records in astronomy from Babylonia, but that 'the art of mathematical demonstration was, almost wholly, Greek in origin.' He frames the chapter's astronomical narrative against the political decline of later Hellenistic Greece: after Archimedes and Apollonius in the third century BC, 'though respectable work continued to be done in Alexandria, the great age was ended,' as Roman domination replaced Greek political liberty and, with it, the self-confidence needed for continued original inquiry.
philosophical_problems: What made Greek mathematics distinctive: not merely calculation, but the invention of rigorous deductive demonstration from explicit axioms.
Can quantities that cannot be exactly measured (irrationals, areas bounded by curves) still be handled with mathematical rigor?
How much confidence can an axiomatic deductive system place in its own starting assumptions?
How was the size, shape, and structure of the cosmos correctly (and incorrectly) inferred from indirect observational evidence?
Why did the ancient world reject Aristarchus's essentially correct heliocentric hypothesis for so long?

philosophers_discussed.name: Eudoxus of Cnidus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Invented the geometrical theory of proportion (freeing the theory from restriction to rational quantities) and either invented or perfected the 'method of exhaustion,' an anticipation of the integral calculus later used with great success by Archimedes.

philosophers_discussed.name: Euclid
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Working at Alexandria around 300 BC, he organized geometry into the axiomatic-deductive system of the Elements; Russell credits him less with original content than with the 'order of propositions, and the logical structure,' calling the result 'one of the greatest books ever written.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans (including Philolaus)
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Credited with first proposing a spherical earth (on aesthetic grounds later given scientific support), with the doctrine that the earth is one of the planets, and with the elaborate 'central fire' cosmology attributed to Philolaus, which Russell treats as a crucial imaginative step toward the Copernican hypothesis despite its fancifulness.

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristarchus of Samos
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: 'The most interesting of all ancient astronomers,' who advanced the complete Copernican hypothesis -- that the earth and all the planets revolve around the sun, and that the earth rotates daily on its axis -- roughly eighteen centuries before Copernicus.

philosophers_discussed.name: Hipparchus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Described by Heath as 'the greatest astronomer of antiquity'; rejected Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis in favor of an improved geocentric theory of epicycles, which became, via Ptolemy, the dominant astronomical system for over a millennium.

philosophers_discussed.name: Archimedes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Applied Eudoxus's method of exhaustion to calculate areas (squaring the parabola exactly) and to bound the value of pi; also the chief surviving witness, via a letter to King Gelon, to Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis; killed when Rome captured Syracuse in 212 BC.

core_concepts.name: The method of exhaustion (an anticipation of the calculus)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: To find the area of a circle, you can inscribe a regular polygon with more and more sides -- a hexagon, then a shape with a thousand sides, then a million -- and the polygon's area gets closer and closer to the circle's true area; the 'method of exhaustion,' invented or perfected by Eudoxus, made this idea mathematically rigorous, and Archimedes used it to get remarkably accurate results.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A technique, developed by Eudoxus and extensively used by Archimedes, for rigorously establishing the area or other measure of a curved figure by showing that inscribed (or circumscribed) polygonal approximations can be made to differ from the true figure by less than any previously assigned quantity, using the 'axiom of Archimedes' (that repeated halving of a quantity eventually produces a value smaller than any given quantity) -- an early anticipation of the integral calculus.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It allowed the Greeks to obtain exact results for some curved figures (Archimedes exactly 'squared' the parabola) and rigorously bounded approximations for others (Archimedes proved pi lies strictly between 3 1/7 and 3 10/71), anticipating methods not formalized again until the calculus of the seventeenth century.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Invented or perfected by Eudoxus (ca. 408-ca. 355 BC), building on his new, more general theory of proportion.
examples: Archimedes used a regular polygon of ninety-six sides, inscribed and circumscribed about a circle, to prove pi is less than 3 1/7 and greater than 3 10/71.
The use of inscribed and circumscribed polygons for approximating pi traces back to Antiphon, a contemporary of Socrates.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: A genuine anticipation of the integral calculus, not matched in rigor again until the seventeenth century.

core_concepts.name: Euclid's axiomatic-deductive method
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Euclid's Elements did not invent most of the individual facts of geometry, but it organized them, for the first time, into a single rigorous system: starting from a small set of explicit definitions and assumptions (including the famous, controversial postulate of parallels), every later result is proved step by step by strict logical deduction.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The method, organized by Euclid around 300 BC, of deriving the whole body of geometrical and (in Book X) proto-algebraic knowledge from an explicit, minimal set of definitions and postulates through rigorous deductive proof, culminating in the construction of the five regular solids; Russell praises both 'rigour in deduction' and Euclid's honesty in 'not concealing the dubiousness of the initial assumption' in the parallel postulate specifically.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It became, in Russell's words, 'one of the greatest books ever written, and one of the most perfect monuments of the Greek intellect,' and remained, into Russell's own lifetime ('when I was young'), the standard schoolboy textbook of geometry.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Compiled by Euclid at Alexandria, shortly after the deaths of Alexander and Aristotle, drawing on and systematizing earlier work including Eudoxus's theory of proportion and Theaetetus's theory of the regular solids.
examples: The theory of proportion in Euclid, following Eudoxus, avoids all the difficulties connected with irrationals 'by methods essentially similar to those introduced by Weierstrass into nineteenth-century analysis.'
objections: Russell: the method is 'purely deductive,' with 'no way, within it, of testing the initial assumptions'; nineteenth-century non-Euclidean geometry showed these assumptions (especially the parallel postulate) 'might be in part mistaken,' decidable ultimately only by observation, not pure reason.
competing_positions: Non-Euclidean geometries, developed in the nineteenth century, which showed alternatives to Euclid's parallel postulate are logically consistent.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Served as the model of rigorous deductive science for over two thousand years; Russell notes it was slow to reach the Latin West, arriving via Arabic translation and Athelhard of Bath's 1120 Latin translation, with important further advances only in the late Renaissance.

core_concepts.name: The Pythagorean 'central fire' cosmology
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A group of Pythagoreans, attributed to Philolaus, proposed that the earth is not the center of the universe but one of ten heavenly bodies (including a hypothetical 'counter-earth') all orbiting a central fire, invisible to the Mediterranean world because the earth always turns the same face away from it -- a scheme that was largely wrong in its details but that made the crucial imaginative leap of removing the earth from the center of the cosmos.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The cosmological system attributed to Philolaus (late fifth century BC), in which the earth, sun, moon, five known planets, a hypothetical counter-earth, and a central fire ('the house of Zeus') together made up ten heavenly bodies (matching the mystically significant Pythagorean number ten), all orbiting the central fire, with the earth rotating so as to keep its inhabited face perpetually turned away from it, and the sun shining by light reflected from the central fire.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls it 'very important, since it involves the greater part of the imaginative effort required for conceiving the Copernican hypothesis': displacing the earth from the cosmic center, even fancifully and for mixed scientific and numerological reasons, was the psychologically difficult step, after which 'it was not so very difficult to be led by scientific arguments to a more accurate theory.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Attributed to Philolaus, a Theban Pythagorean of the late fifth century BC.
examples: The counter-earth's postulated existence rested partly on a genuine observation (a lunar eclipse sometimes occurring while both sun and moon are above the horizon, actually caused by refraction, unknown to the Pythagoreans) and partly on numerology (needing exactly ten heavenly bodies).
objections: The central fire and counter-earth were themselves dropped by later Pythagoreans, soon after Plato's time, once observational astronomy advanced further.
competing_positions: The traditional geocentric picture it displaced, and the later, more scientifically grounded heliocentric hypothesis of Aristarchus that built on its central insight.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Prepared the conceptual ground for Heraclides's and, above all, Aristarchus's later heliocentric proposals.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The central fire was given the religious names 'the house of Zeus' and 'the Mother of the gods,' reflecting its Pythagorean-mystical, not purely astronomical, motivation.

core_concepts.name: Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Around the early third century BC, Aristarchus of Samos proposed that the sun stands still at the center while the earth and all the other planets revolve around it, and that the earth also spins on its own axis once a day -- essentially the full Copernican theory, roughly eighteen hundred years before Copernicus, though it was rejected by nearly all other ancient astronomers.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The hypothesis, attested chiefly by Archimedes's letter to King Gelon and by Plutarch, Aëtius, and Sextus Empiricus, that the fixed stars and the sun remain unmoved while the earth revolves about the sun in a circular orbit and simultaneously rotates on its own axis; adopted only tentatively, or perhaps only as a calculating device, by Aristarchus himself in his sole surviving work, but adopted as definite fact by his successor Seleucus around 150 BC.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It shows that the essential Copernican insight was available to ancient science far earlier than commonly assumed, and its near-total rejection by later antiquity (mainly due to Hipparchus) illustrates how observational sophistication and theoretical correctness do not automatically go together.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Advanced by Aristarchus of Samos (ca. 310-230 BC), roughly twenty-five years older than Archimedes.
examples: Archimedes reports Aristarchus's hypotheses directly: 'the fixed stars and the sun remain unmoved, that the earth revolves about the sun in the circumference of a circle, the sun lying in the middle of the orbit.'

Cleanthes reportedly thought Aristarchus should be indicted for impiety for 'putting in motion the Hearth of the Universe' (the earth) -- evidence, Russell notes, of the religious pressure that may have made Aristarchus cautious about stating the hypothesis as more than tentative.
objections: Aristarchus's only surviving work, On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and the Moon, uses geocentric assumptions throughout; Sir Thomas Heath, whom Russell follows, suggests this may reflect either calculational convenience (the choice of frame makes no difference to that book's specific problems) or that Aristarchus arrived at the heliocentric view only after writing it.
competing_positions: Hipparchus's later, more influential geocentric epicycle theory, which prevailed over Aristarchus's hypothesis for the remainder of antiquity and the Middle Ages.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Copernicus knew of Aristarchus's hypothesis and 'was encouraged by finding ancient authority for his innovation,' though Russell notes its effect on the intervening centuries of astronomy was 'practically nil.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Cleanthes's threatened charge of impiety against Aristarchus shows heliocentrism could be seen as religiously transgressive in antiquity, just as it would be again for Galileo.

core_concepts.name: Hipparchus and the epicycle theory (toward the Ptolemaic system)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Hipparchus, called by the historian Heath 'the greatest astronomer of antiquity,' rejected Aristarchus's sun-centered theory and instead refined an alternative geocentric model using 'epicycles' -- circles moving on circles -- which later astronomers developed into the complex, earth-centered Ptolemaic system that dominated astronomy for over a thousand years.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Hipparchus's (fl. 161-126 BC) adoption and improvement of the epicycle theory (originally invented by Apollonius, fl. ca. 220 BC) as a geocentric alternative to Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis, combined with genuinely major achievements -- the first systematic trigonometry, discovery of the precession of the equinoxes, a highly accurate lunar month estimate, improved sun/moon distance estimates, and a catalogue of 850 fixed stars -- whose cumulative authority caused the heliocentric hypothesis to be set aside until Copernicus.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Hipparchus's work, later systematized by Ptolemy (fl. mid-second century AD) into what became known as the Ptolemaic system, was largely responsible for the 'general rejection' of Aristarchus's correct heliocentric hypothesis for roughly seventeen centuries.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Hipparchus, building on Apollonius's earlier invention of epicycles.
examples: Hipparchus estimated the length of the lunar month with an error of less than one second.
He catalogued eight hundred and fifty fixed stars, giving their latitude and longitude.
competing_positions: Aristarchus's and Seleucus's heliocentric hypothesis, which the epicycle tradition displaced for the remainder of antiquity.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Developed by Ptolemy into the 'Ptolemaic system,' the dominant astronomical model in the West and the Islamic world until Copernicus.

core_concepts.name: 'Saving the phenomena': Greek astronomy as geometrical, not dynamic
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Ancient Greek astronomers did not think in terms of physical forces pushing and pulling the planets, as Newton later would; instead, they tried to find the simplest possible geometrical arrangement (circles, and circles upon circles) that would correctly predict the observed positions of the heavenly bodies -- a method Russell says was, in a real sense, scientifically correct even though it lacked the concept of force.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's characterization of the ancient astronomical problem as essentially geometrical: given only the apparent two-dimensional motions of heavenly bodies on the celestial sphere, hypothesize a third coordinate (depth) so as to make the resulting description as simple as possible, without appeal to physical force, a method Russell says the Greeks pursued 'in effect, though not altogether in intention... in the scientifically correct way,' and which he notes curiously resurfaces, with force again 'banished,' in Einstein's General Theory of Relativity.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It reframes the merit of the Copernican hypothesis itself: Russell argues its merit 'is not truth, but simplicity,' since, given the relativity of motion, no absolute question of truth is strictly at issue in choosing a reference frame.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A pattern Russell identifies across the whole tradition from the Pythagoreans through Hipparchus and Ptolemy.
examples: The Ptolemaic and Copernican systems alike used only uniform circular motions or compounds of circular motions, with 'spheres' carrying the heavenly bodies, lacking any concept of force.
competing_positions: Newton's dynamic, force-based astronomy ('a new point of view, less geometrical'), later echoed, in a partial reversal, by Einstein's geometrical General Theory of Relativity.

arguments.title: Aristotle's argument against Anaximander on the earth's immobility
premises: Anaximander held the earth floats freely, unsupported, remaining still at the center because there is no more reason for it to move in one direction than another.
Aristotle analogizes this to a man placed equidistant from identical piles of food around a circle, with no reason to choose one pile over another.
arguments.conclusion: Such a man, lacking any reason to choose, would starve to death -- implying, Aristotle suggests, that Anaximander's 'no reason to move' argument is absurd, since (Aristotle implies) some other explanation for the earth's stability must be found.
arguments.explanation: Russell notes this argument, originally about cosmology, 'reappears in scholastic philosophy, not in connection with astronomy, but with free will,' in the medieval form of 'Buridan's ass,' unable to choose between two equally attractive bundles of hay and therefore starving.
implications: Illustrates how an argument-form can migrate from one philosophical domain (cosmology) to an entirely different one (free will) across many centuries.

arguments.title: The Pythagorean argument for a spherical earth from lunar eclipse shadows
premises: Anaxagoras had already discovered that lunar eclipses are caused by the earth's shadow falling on the moon.
The observed shape of the earth's shadow during a lunar eclipse is consistently curved, matching the outline of a sphere.
arguments.conclusion: The earth must be spherical, giving the Pythagoreans (who had already favored this view on aesthetic grounds) a genuine scientific argument for it.
arguments.explanation: Russell notes Pythagoras himself 'was, in all probability, the first to think the earth spherical,' though his reasons were originally 'aesthetic rather than scientific'; the eclipse-shadow observation supplied the scientific confirmation.
implications: Set the stage for the Pythagorean move to treat the earth as one planet among others, a necessary step toward the later central-fire and heliocentric hypotheses.

arguments.title: Archimedes's exhaustion-method proof bounding pi
premises: A regular polygon inscribed in a circle has an area proportional to the square of the circle's diameter, and its area approaches the circle's area as the number of sides increases.
The 'axiom of Archimedes' guarantees that, by repeated halving, a difference can always be made smaller than any previously assigned quantity.
Using both an inscribed and a circumscribed regular polygon of ninety-six sides, upper and lower numerical bounds on the circle's area (and hence on pi) can be computed directly.
arguments.conclusion: Pi is strictly less than 3 1/7 and strictly greater than 3 10/71.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as a paradigm case of the method of exhaustion in action, showing how a problem (squaring the circle) that cannot be solved exactly can nonetheless be resolved into a rigorously bounded approximation, 'and that is all that any method can do in this problem.'
implications: Demonstrates the genuine rigor achievable within Greek mathematics even for problems, like squaring the circle, that admit no exact solution by their methods.

key_distinctions: Practical, rule-of-thumb mathematics (Egyptian/Babylonian) vs. rigorous demonstrative mathematics (Greek innovation)
The arithmetical theory of proportion (restricted to rational quantities) vs. Eudoxus's geometrical theory of proportion (applicable to irrationals as well)
Exact results obtainable by the method of exhaustion (e.g., squaring the parabola) vs. results only approximable to arbitrary precision (e.g., squaring the circle)
A geocentric universe (traditional, and later the Ptolemaic system) vs. a heliocentric universe (Aristarchus, Seleucus, and eventually Copernicus)
Geometrical astronomy (uniform circular motions, no concept of force) vs. dynamic astronomy (Newtonian forces, later echoed geometrically again in Einstein's relativity)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell traces Eudoxus's theory of proportion and method of exhaustion as responses to the earlier (Pythagorean) discovery of irrational magnitudes, and shows Euclid's Elements building directly on Eudoxus's proportion theory and on Theaetetus's completed theory of the regular solids (already discussed in connection with Plato's Timaeus). He also connects Aristotle's cosmological objection to Anaximander directly back to Presocratic material covered in earlier chapters, and traces the whole heliocentric tradition (Pythagoras, Philolaus's central fire, Heraclides, Aristarchus, Seleucus) as a continuous sequence of increasingly accurate departures from naive geocentrism.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell draws an extended parallel between Euclid's theory of proportion and the nineteenth-century analytic methods of Weierstrass, notes that nineteenth-century non-Euclidean geometry vindicated Euclid's own honesty about the 'dubiousness' of the parallel postulate, and traces the transmission of Euclid's Elements from Alexandria through Arabic translation (under Harun al-Rashid) to Athelhard of Bath's 1120 Latin translation and eventual Renaissance revival. He also connects Aristarchus's rejected heliocentric hypothesis directly to Copernicus, who found 'encouragement' in its ancient precedent, and notes a 'curious' partial reversion to purely geometrical (force-free) astronomy in Einstein's General Theory of Relativity, after the intervening Newtonian dynamic interlude.
political_social_context: Russell frames the end of the great age of Greek mathematics and astronomy in explicitly political terms: after Archimedes and Apollonius, Roman domination caused the Greeks to lose 'the self-confidence that belongs to political liberty,' replacing it with 'a paralysing respect for their predecessors'; the killing of Archimedes by a Roman soldier during the capture of Syracuse in 212 BC is presented as 'a symbol of the death of original thought that Rome caused throughout the Hellenic world.'
religion_science_culture_context: Russell notes the Pythagorean central-fire cosmology was bound up with religious and numerological motivations (the mystic significance of the number ten, the central fire's names 'the house of Zeus' and 'the Mother of the gods'), and that Cleanthes reportedly wished to prosecute Aristarchus for impiety over the heliocentric hypothesis -- a preview, seventeen centuries early, of the religious controversy that would later confront Galileo.
russell_presentation: Russell frames the whole chapter as concerned with mathematics and astronomy specifically 'as related to Greek philosophy,' not as independent technical history. He opens with anecdotes illustrating practical stimuli to mathematics (Thales and the pyramid's shadow, the distance of a ship at sea, the oracle's demand to double a cube-shaped offering, which occupied Plato's Academy for generations) before turning to the serious mathematical content: the discovery of irrational magnitudes and Eudoxus's resulting geometrical theory of proportion and method of exhaustion, exemplified by Archimedes's bounding of pi; Euclid's organization of geometry into a rigorous axiomatic system, its later historical transmission via the Arabic-speaking world into the Latin West, and Russell's own assessment of its strengths (rigor) and limitations (no internal test of its own assumptions); and finally an extended astronomical narrative moving from Babylonian and Egyptian observational groundwork, through Anaximander, Pythagoras, and the Pythagorean central-fire cosmology of Philolaus, to Heraclides's discovery that Venus and Mercury orbit the sun, to Aristarchus's full heliocentric hypothesis and its rejection in favor of Hipparchus's and Ptolemy's geocentric epicycle theory, closing with a comparative table of ancient estimates of the sun's distance and Russell's own reflection on the geometrical, force-free character of ancient astronomy as a whole.
critical_context: Russell repeatedly supplies his own interpretive framing rather than simply reporting facts: he argues that the Copernican hypothesis's true merit 'is not truth, but simplicity,' given the relativity of motion; he credits ancient astronomers with 'in effect... tackling the problem in the scientifically correct way' despite lacking the concept of force; and he closes with an explicitly political explanation (loss of self-confidence under Roman rule) for why the 'great age' of Greek mathematics ended when it did, rather than attributing the end to any purely intellectual exhaustion. He is also careful to flag interpretive uncertainty where the ancient evidence itself is ambiguous, as in Aristarchus's own surviving (geocentric-framed) treatise, following Sir Thomas Heath's scholarly judgment rather than presenting a settled consensus as fact.
key_takeaways: The Greeks' distinctive mathematical achievement was not calculation itself (borrowed in part from Egypt and Babylon) but the invention of rigorous deductive demonstration from explicit axioms.

Eudoxus's geometrical theory of proportion and 'method of exhaustion' resolved the crisis caused by the discovery of irrational magnitudes and anticipated the integral calculus, later used by Archimedes to bound the value of pi exactly.

Euclid's Elements organized geometry into a rigorous axiomatic-deductive system; Russell praises its logical rigor while noting it has 'no way, within it, of testing the initial assumptions,' a limitation exposed by nineteenth-century non-Euclidean geometry.

The Pythagorean 'central fire' cosmology, though largely wrong in its details, made the crucial imaginative step of displacing the earth from the cosmic center, preparing the ground for later heliocentric theories.

Aristarchus of Samos proposed the full Copernican heliocentric hypothesis roughly eighteen centuries before Copernicus, but it was rejected by later antiquity, chiefly due to Hipparchus's influential geocentric epicycle theory, which developed into the dominant Ptolemaic system.

Russell attributes the end of the 'great age' of Greek mathematics and astronomy, after Archimedes and Apollonius, to the political consequences of Roman domination rather than to any purely intellectual cause.
study_notes:
This chapter has two roughly parallel halves -- mathematics, then astronomy -- and both follow the same underlying narrative shape: an early conceptual breakthrough, followed by a long period in which the correct or most promising idea is set aside in favor of a less adequate but more socially or observationally entrenched alternative. In mathematics, this shows up as the tension between exact deductive rigor (Euclid's axiomatic method) and the problem of unprovable starting assumptions (only resolved, much later, by non-Euclidean geometry). In astronomy, it shows up even more dramatically: Aristarchus got the right answer (heliocentrism) in the third century BC, and the ancient world still spent the next several centuries systematizing an elaborate alternative (Hipparchus's and Ptolemy's epicycles) that turned out to be wrong. Understanding why -- calculational convenience, religious pressure, and Hipparchus's genuinely superior observational achievements in other respects -- is the chapter's central interpretive payoff.

When you reach the Aristarchus material, note carefully how Russell handles the historical evidence: rather than simply asserting 'Aristarchus discovered heliocentrism,' he walks through the specific ancient sources (Archimedes's letter to Gelon, Plutarch's report of Cleanthes's threatened impiety charge, Aëtius, Sextus Empiricus) that establish this, and flags the genuine scholarly uncertainty (via Heath) about how firmly Aristarchus himself held the view, given that his one surviving book uses geocentric assumptions. This is a good model for how to reason carefully from fragmentary ancient evidence rather than overstating certainty.

Finally, connect Russell's closing point about 'saving the phenomena' back to his treatment of Plato's own aesthetic bias toward circular celestial motion (covered several chapters earlier, in connection with the theory of Ideas): both passages make the same broader point about the history of science -- that a hypothesis's usefulness in prompting discovery is a separate question from its ultimate truth, and that Greek astronomy's purely geometrical, force-free method was, in its own way, a genuinely productive scientific strategy even without the concept of force.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A technique for finding the area of a curved shape (like a circle) by fitting many-sided polygons inside and outside it, getting closer and closer to the true area.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A rigorous technique, developed by Eudoxus and used extensively by Archimedes, for establishing the measure of a curved figure via polygonal approximations that can be made to differ from the true value by less than any assigned quantity, anticipating the integral calculus.
related_concepts: The method of exhaustion (an anticipation of the calculus)

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The principle that if you keep halving a quantity, you will eventually get something smaller than any amount you name in advance.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The principle (used in the method of exhaustion) that for any two quantities a > b, there exists some whole number n such that repeated halving of a, n times, yields a quantity smaller than b, guaranteeing convergence of polygonal approximations.
related_concepts: The method of exhaustion (an anticipation of the calculus)

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Euclid's assumption about parallel lines, which he could not prove from his other axioms but stated openly rather than hiding.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The fifth postulate of Euclid's Elements, whose independence from Euclid's other axioms was suspected for centuries and confirmed only by the development of non-Euclidean geometries in the nineteenth century.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: In an early Pythagorean theory, a fire at the center of the universe that the earth and other planets orbit, always hidden from the inhabited world.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The central body of Philolaus's Pythagorean cosmology, around which ten heavenly bodies (including earth and a hypothetical counter-earth) were held to revolve, with the earth's rotation keeping the Mediterranean world perpetually turned away from it.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A circle whose center moves along the edge of another circle, used by ancient astronomers to model the complicated apparent paths of the planets while keeping the earth at the center.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A geometrical device, invented by Apollonius and developed by Hipparchus and Ptolemy, in which a planet moves on a small circle (epicycle) whose center in turn moves on a larger circle (deferent) around the earth, used to preserve geocentrism while matching observed planetary motion.
related_concepts: Hipparchus and the epicycle theory (toward the Ptolemaic system)

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The theory that the sun, not the earth, is at the center of the solar system, with the earth and planets orbiting it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The astronomical hypothesis, advanced by Aristarchus of Samos and later adopted as definite by Seleucus, that the sun remains fixed while the earth and other planets revolve around it in circular orbits, with the earth additionally rotating daily on its own axis.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes Greek mathematics from the Egyptian and Babylonian mathematics it partly drew on, according to Russell?
questions.answer: The Greeks derived practical rules of thumb from Egypt and long observational records from Babylonia, but the art of rigorous mathematical demonstration -- proving results deductively from explicit assumptions -- was 'almost wholly' a Greek invention.
questions.explanation: This distinction frames the whole chapter's treatment of both mathematics and astronomy.

questions.prompt: What is the 'method of exhaustion,' and what problem did it allow Archimedes to solve regarding pi?
questions.answer: A technique using inscribed and circumscribed polygons, made increasingly many-sided, to approximate the area of curved figures to arbitrary precision; using a 96-sided polygon, Archimedes proved pi is strictly between 3 1/7 and 3 10/71.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as a genuine anticipation of the integral calculus.

questions.prompt: What does Russell identify as both the great strength and the great limitation of Euclid's axiomatic method?
questions.answer: Its strength is rigor in deduction from explicit assumptions; its limitation is that it provides 'no way, within it, of testing the initial assumptions,' a limitation later exposed by nineteenth-century non-Euclidean geometry, which showed Euclid's assumptions might be only partly correct.
questions.explanation: Russell praises Euclid for openly acknowledging the 'dubiousness' of the parallel postulate rather than concealing it.

questions.prompt: Compare the Pythagorean 'central fire' cosmology with Aristarchus's later heliocentric hypothesis. What did the earlier theory contribute to the later one, despite its own errors?
questions.answer: The central fire cosmology wrongly kept the earth off-center around a fictitious central fire rather than the sun, and included a fictitious counter-earth; but its crucial contribution, per Russell, was the imaginative step of removing the earth from the cosmic center altogether, which Aristarchus's later, more scientifically accurate sun-centered hypothesis built upon.
questions.explanation: Russell calls the central-fire theory responsible for 'the greater part of the imaginative effort required for conceiving the Copernican hypothesis.'

questions.prompt: Who first advanced the complete heliocentric hypothesis in antiquity, and who is credited with adopting it as definite fact rather than mere hypothesis?
questions.answer: Aristarchus of Samos advanced it (possibly tentatively); his successor Seleucus, around 150 BC, maintained it as a definite opinion.
questions.explanation: This distinction matters because Aristarchus's own surviving work uses geocentric assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why was Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis largely rejected by later ancient astronomers?
questions.answer: Mainly because of Hipparchus, called 'the greatest astronomer of antiquity,' who adopted and improved the geocentric epicycle theory instead, later developed by Ptolemy into the dominant Ptolemaic system that prevailed until Copernicus.
questions.explanation: Russell notes Aristarchus's influence on the intervening centuries of astronomy was 'practically nil.'

questions.prompt: What political explanation does Russell give for the end of the 'great age' of Greek mathematics after Archimedes and Apollonius?
questions.answer: Roman domination caused the Greeks to lose the self-confidence that belongs to political liberty, replacing it with a 'paralysing respect for their predecessors'; the Roman soldier who killed Archimedes symbolizes the death of original thought that Rome caused throughout the Hellenic world.
questions.explanation: This closes the chapter on an explicitly political, rather than purely intellectual, note.

flashcards.front: What is distinctively Greek about Greek mathematics, according to Russell?
flashcards.back: Not calculation itself (partly borrowed from Egypt and Babylon) but the invention of rigorous mathematical demonstration from explicit axioms.

flashcards.front: Who invented or perfected the 'method of exhaustion,' and who later used it to great effect?
flashcards.back: Eudoxus of Cnidus invented or perfected it; Archimedes used it extensively, including to bound the value of pi.

flashcards.front: What bounds did Archimedes prove for the value of pi?
flashcards.back: Strictly less than 3 1/7 and strictly greater than 3 10/71, using inscribed and circumscribed 96-sided polygons.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's overall verdict on Euclid's Elements?
flashcards.back: 'One of the greatest books ever written, and one of the most perfect monuments of the Greek intellect,' though purely deductive and unable to test its own initial assumptions.

flashcards.front: What did nineteenth-century non-Euclidean geometry show about Euclid's parallel postulate?
flashcards.back: That it might be only in part mistaken, and that only observation, not pure reason, could decide the true geometry of physical space.

flashcards.front: Who first translated Euclid's Elements into Latin, and roughly when?
flashcards.back: Athelhard of Bath, from an Arabic translation, in 1120 AD -- the first still-extant Latin translation.

flashcards.front: What is the Pythagorean 'central fire' cosmology, and to whom is it attributed?
flashcards.back: A system (attributed to Philolaus) in which the earth is one of ten heavenly bodies orbiting a central fire, rather than the fixed center of the universe.

flashcards.front: Why does Russell consider the central-fire cosmology important, despite its errors?
flashcards.back: Because it made the crucial imaginative step of displacing the earth from the cosmic center, paving the way for later heliocentric theories.

flashcards.front: Who advanced the full Copernican heliocentric hypothesis in antiquity, and roughly when?
flashcards.back: Aristarchus of Samos, around 310-230 BC -- about eighteen centuries before Copernicus.

flashcards.front: Who is our chief ancient source of evidence for Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis?
flashcards.back: Archimedes, in a letter to King Gelon of Syracuse.

flashcards.front: Who threatened to indict Aristarchus for impiety, and why?
flashcards.back: Cleanthes, for 'putting in motion the Hearth of the Universe' (the earth) by proposing heliocentrism.

flashcards.front: Who is credited with adopting Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis as definite fact rather than mere hypothesis?
Whose work caused the general rejection of heliocentrism in later antiquity, and what system resulted?
flashcards.back: Hipparchus's, whose improved geocentric epicycle theory was later developed by Ptolemy into the dominant Ptolemaic system.

flashcards.front: What does Russell say is the true merit of the Copernican (heliocentric) hypothesis, given the relativity of motion?
flashcards.back: Simplicity, not truth -- since, given the relativity of motion, no absolute question of truth is strictly at stake in the choice of reference frame.

flashcards.front: What political explanation does Russell give for the end of the great age of Greek mathematics?
flashcards.back: Roman domination caused the Greeks to lose the self-confidence of political liberty, replacing it with excessive deference to their predecessors.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, what was distinctively Greek about Greek mathematics?
options: Rigorous mathematical demonstration from explicit axioms
The invention of the number zero
quiz.explanation: Rules of thumb came from Egypt and observational records from Babylon; rigorous demonstration was Greek.

quiz.prompt: The 'method of exhaustion' is described by Russell as an anticipation of the integral calculus.
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly calls it 'an anticipation of the integral calculus.'
quiz.related_concept: The method of exhaustion (an anticipation of the calculus)

quiz.prompt: Who organized geometry into the rigorous axiomatic system of the Elements?
quiz.explanation: Euclid compiled the Elements at Alexandria around 300 BC.

quiz.prompt: Nineteenth-century ___ geometry showed that Euclid's parallel postulate might be only in part mistaken.
quiz.explanation: Non-Euclidean geometry demonstrated alternatives to the parallel postulate are logically consistent.

quiz.prompt: What was the significance of the Pythagorean 'central fire' cosmology, according to Russell, despite its factual errors?
options: It correctly calculated the earth's diameter
It made the crucial imaginative step of displacing the earth from the cosmic center
It proved the earth was flat
It disproved the existence of other planets
quiz.explanation: Russell credits it with most of the imaginative work needed to later conceive heliocentrism.

quiz.prompt: Aristarchus of Samos advanced the full heliocentric hypothesis roughly eighteen centuries before Copernicus.
quiz.explanation: Aristarchus (ca. 310-230 BC) proposed the essentially Copernican hypothesis far earlier.

quiz.prompt: Who is our chief surviving ancient source of direct evidence for Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis?
options: Archimedes, in a letter to King Gelon
quiz.explanation: Archimedes reports Aristarchus's hypotheses directly in a letter to Gelon of Syracuse.

quiz.prompt: Why was Aristarchus's heliocentric hypothesis largely rejected in later antiquity?
options: Hipparchus's improved geocentric epicycle theory, later systematized by Ptolemy, prevailed instead
No ancient source ever recorded it
quiz.explanation: Hipparchus's epicycle-based system, developed into the Ptolemaic system, displaced Aristarchus's hypothesis for centuries.
quiz.related_concept: Hipparchus and the epicycle theory (toward the Ptolemaic system)

quiz.prompt: Match each figure to their key astronomical contribution: (1) Hipparchus, (2) Heraclides of Pontus, (3) Seleucus.
options: Hipparchus ~ improved geocentric epicycle theory and star catalogue; Heraclides ~ discovered Venus and Mercury orbit the sun and the earth rotates daily; Seleucus ~ adopted heliocentrism as definite fact
Hipparchus ~ first proposed heliocentrism; Heraclides ~ built the Ptolemaic system; Seleucus ~ discovered the precession of the equinoxes
All three rejected the sphericity of the earth
Hipparchus ~ discovered irrational numbers; Heraclides ~ invented epicycles; Seleucus ~ translated Euclid into Latin
quiz.explanation: Each astronomer made a distinct, specific contribution described in the chapter.

quiz.prompt: Russell attributes the end of the great age of Greek mathematics primarily to a purely intellectual exhaustion of ideas.
quiz.explanation: Russell attributes it to the political consequences of Roman domination, which undermined Greek self-confidence.
quiz.related_concept: 'Saving the phenomena': Greek astronomy as geometrical, not dynamic

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's claim that the Copernican hypothesis's true merit is 'simplicity, not truth,' given the relativity of motion. Does this claim adequately capture what is scientifically significant about the shift from geocentrism to heliocentrism?
rubric: Explains the relativity-of-motion premise behind it
Considers a counterargument (e.g., dynamical/causal reasons to prefer heliocentrism, such as Newtonian gravitation)

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze why Aristarchus's correct heliocentric hypothesis was rejected by later antiquity in favor of Hipparchus's and Ptolemy's geocentric epicycle system. What combination of observational, religious, and institutional factors does Russell identify?
rubric: Accurately describes Aristarchus's hypothesis and its evidence
Accurately describes Hipparchus's competing achievements and epicycle theory
Identifies at least one non-purely-scientific factor (e.g., Cleanthes's impiety charge)

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Euclid's axiomatic-deductive method with the method of exhaustion as two different Greek mathematical achievements. What kind of certainty does each provide, and what are the limits of each, according to Russell?
rubric: Accurately describes Euclid's method and its documented limitation (untestable initial assumptions)
Accurately describes the method of exhaustion and its documented limitation (approximation rather than exactness in cases like squaring the circle)
Compares the two methods' relative strengths
Uses specific textual detail from the chapter
